title: Updated Canyon Grail gets real-world fast and a huge bump in tyre clearance
content:
Cyclist
Updated Canyon Grail gets real-world fast and a huge bump in tyre clearance

The new Canyon Grail is positioned as a wide tired, aero-focused, super-compliant race bike that doesn’t neglect the consumers who don’t want to race it.

Once home to the whacky hover bar system and fairly conservative design elsewhere, the Grail has evolved into an out and out modern gravel race bike. But that doesn’t mean it’s not a bike you can use to explore or live with on the daily.

Updating the OG

The Canyon Grail was the brand’s first introduction to gravel bikes, with the Grizl following shortly afterwards positioned as a more traditional gravel bike for exploring rather than racing. With the double stacked hover-bar, the original Grail was not afraid of doing things differently, but as the gravel race scene has evolved rapidly, so too have the requirements needed for a capable gravel race bike.

To that end, Canyon have completely revamped the Grail, with it now sharing a lot of design similarities with both the Aeroad aero road frame, and the 2026 Endurace CFR frame as gravel race speeds verge on the same sort of speeds seen on the road just over half a decade ago.

This means internal cable routing, a one-piece aero bar and stem, tear drop tube profiles everywhere and stocked with deep section rims. But of course, being for gravel, tyre clearances are up, internal storage is in, in-built compliance is plenty, and the front mech is gone.

What has changed on the new Canyon Grail?

The headline change on the new Canyon Grail is the 57mm tyre clearance both front and rear, with 4mm additional clearance to allow for mud clogging and shedding without damage to the frame. This is clearly in-line with the latest aero gravel race frames from Argon 18 and Ridley, and exceeds beyond what the Specialized Crux 5 is capable of. With more and more gravel racers seeking wider tyres for reduced rolling resistance and increased comfort, this was a must have feature of the frame. However, it also opens up the potential for the frame to be used for more adventure riding, as with the similarly equipped 57mm tyre clearance Scott Addict Gravel that was also released this year.

In addition to this the geometry has been tweaked to make the wheelbase longer and the front end significantly lower, a byproduct of race speeds getting higher and riders wanting to reduce their frontal area while maintaining control over rough terrain. The Pace bar from the Aeroad has also been adopted, allowing for geometry changes without the need for cable rerouting, as well as fitments such as clip-on extensions for those racing events such as Badlands.

Storage is also expanded with internal frame storage, as well as a partnership with Cyclite to make lightweight and aerodynamic frame and top-tube storage solutions, something a few bike brands have cottoned onto this year. A new GR 50 CF carbon wheelset has also been released with the frame, focusing on aero performance for wide tyres without excessive weight. And for those who want a practical bike, fender mounts are included to fit the Defend Fast Fenders from Canyon, something often lacking in more aero gravel race frames, although not present on the CFR frame.

With a CFR, CF SLX, and CF model range available, Canyon has aimed to make the new Grail suitable for both high end racers, and those wanting a bike that can be ridden pretty much anywhere at any time.

Aero takes centre stage

At the heart of the changes to the new Grail, the design methodology that is most clearly visible is a heavy focus on aerodynamics. Canyon states that this frame outperforms the main competitors at 35kmh. Normally, wind tunnel testing figures, even for gravel, tend to use 45kmh. Canyon does this itself, but only for the road. Gravel meanwhile is not raced that fast, so Canyon thought that was a needless speed target to state aero gains. At a far more realistic 35kmh, using the GST Windtunnel in Immenstadt, the new Grail was found to be faster than the Factor Ostro Gravel, Cervelo Aspero 5, and Rose Backroad FF. Of course, this neglects the latest Specialised Crux 5, Argon 18 Anti Matter and Factor Elara, three modern high tyre clearance aero gravel race frames.

A large part of this aero performance comes from the tube shapes, which are highly reminiscent of the 2026 Canyon Endurace CFR, which itself takes heavily from the Canyon Aeroad aero road bike. The down tube is very wide, shielding the bottles but also coming off the back of wider gravel tyres very nicely. Meanwhile the seat tube has the same cutout found on the Endurace CFR.

Another carry over from the aero road division is the adoption of the PACE bar with Gear Groove. This allows users to switch out the drops used, as well as adjust the bar width and bar height without the need to re-route cables or put spacers above the stem, using just a T25 tool. The Control drops allow for a wide 17˚ flare from the tops, giving a balance between a narrow aero position on the hoods, and a wider more stable position on the drops for technical sections of gravel. This bar system also allows for clip-on extensions to be added, ideal for FKTs or events such as Badlands. For those wanting the maximum aero gains, the Race bar be selected at the expense of adjustability.

Even the seatpost is a deep bladed aerofoil shape, although the VCLS insert at the front of the seatpost adds a great deal of compliance. It’s a reverse of the seatpost design used by Scott, where the hollowed out section is at the rear, and having tested that bike this design of seatpost does offer a very comfortable degree of vertical compliance.

Geometry shifts

Of course, no new gravel frame is complete without larger tyre clearances. Canyon has upped the Grail to 57mm clearance, with 4mm of ISO clearance to spare. This means 2.2in tyres can be used happily in the wet without the worry that mud will clog and damage the frame. As gravel racers experiment with wider tyres and wider rims to reduce rolling resistance while maintaining aero performance, this is right at the upper limit of what we are seeing gravel bikes equipped with.

The latest Ridley Kanzo Fast and Argon 18 Anti Matter both feature the same clearances, while the latest Specialized Crux 5 lags at 55mm and Van Rysel RCR-G at a mere 50mm. There is still an argument that 55+mm is excessive, and in some cases not the most efficient tyre choice thanks to aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance on hard-pack or tarmac, and the high rotational mass for steep inclines and accelerations. But having the option for these tyres opens up the possibilities for what this bike can be used for.

This increase in clearance also pairs up with some geometry changes. The front end is dropped 15mm in the pursuit of aggressive race positions and greater aero. Ideal for racers, perhaps not best for adventure riders that this bike is still positioned towards. The Pace bars for example are limited in the amount of stack that can be added to them, with just 20mm maximum from a slammed position.

The wheelbase has also been extended, in part due to the adoption of wider tyres requiring more clearance, but also to increase the stability over rough terrain. Head tube angle and trail are consistent across frame now at 71.5° and 69mm giving a degree of snappiness especially at lower speeds without resulting in a bike that is twitchy when travelling faster.

Storage galore

On all models save the base CF platform, the Grail comes with internal storage in the down tube under the bottle cages. This is commonplace now on most gravel race frames to stash spares and tools without having anything attached externally which can disrupt airflow and impair aerodynamic performance.

Another new addition is the Cyclite partnership which brings about a new waterproof top tube bag and Midloader frame bag. This Midloader is frame size specific so as to work with water bottles and create a bag with no gaps, which had no negative impact on aero performance. These have also been designed to be incredibly lightweight, 200g lighter than the previous version used on the Grail Gen 2. These bags attach to inbuilt bosses on the frame for a clean look with zero straps, similar to the new Argon 18 Antimatter and Scott Addict Gravel.

Another addition that is lacking from many gravel race bike competitors is the option for fenders. Two-bolt fitments are present on all but the CFR frames, and work exclusively with Canyon’s Defend Fast Fenders.

New with the Canyon Grail Gen 3 are the new Canyon GR 50 CF wheelset. 50mm deep, carbon, with 27mm internal and 38.5mm external width, and 1,675g for the pair, they are not the lightest, but an ideal width and depth to use for high speed events or consistent paced ones. At €999 they represent pretty good value and use the very reliable DT Swiss 350 hubs. These wheels are present on two models in the new Grail line-up at present.
